items.text: You said: celldelning mitosis

items.html:
Mitos är den process där en cell delas upp i två genetiskt identiska dotterceller. Denna form av celldelning sker i alla kroppens celler (somatiska celler) utom i könscellerna, och är avgörande för tillväxt och reparation av vävnader. 
Processen delas vanligtvis in i fyra huvudsakliga faser: 
  • Profas: Kromosomerna packas tätt och blir synliga.
  • Metafas: Kromosomerna radar upp sig i cellens mitt (ekvatoriallinjen).
  • Anafas: Syster kromatiderna separeras och dras mot varandras poler.
  • Telofas: Nya kärnmembran bildas runt de två nya cellkärnorna. 
Efter telofasen sker själva celldelningen, som kallas cytokines, där cellmembranet snörs av så att två fristående celler bildas. 
Om du vill kan jag hjälpa dig att fördjupa dig i ämnet. Jag kan till exempel: 
  • Förklara skillnaden mellan mitos och meios (könscelldelning)
  • Beskriva vad som händer i detalj under varje specifik fas
  • Berätta hur cancer är kopplat till okontrollerad celldelning 
Vad skulle du vilja veta mer om?

items.text: You said: yes but mitosis?

items.html:
Ah, my apologies! It seems we took a quick detour into quantum physics. Let’s jump back to biology and mitosis. 
In a way, your concept of a "double Hadamard" actually makes perfect sense for mitosis! Just like the double Hadamard brings you back to your original state, mitosis is a process that duplicates a cell to create two exact copies of the original. 
Here is how that "reset to the original state" works biologically during cell division: 
  • The Starting State: You begin with one mother cell containing a full set of DNA.
  • The Copy Phase (Interphase): Before mitosis even starts, the cell duplicates its DNA so it has two identical copies of everything.
  • The Separation (Mitosis): The cell splits those copies perfectly down the middle.
  • The End Result: You end up with two new cells that are genetically identical to each other and to the original mother cell. 
Unlike quantum states which can be complex mixes, mitosis is nature's way of ensuring that a skin cell makes another identical skin cell, keeping your body's "data" perfectly preserved. 
Would you like to explore how the DNA replicates before the split, or should we look at what triggers a cell to start dividing?

När du nämner "två punkter med en cirkel eromheen" (runt dem), så beskriver du hur en dubbel Hadamard-transformation (eller två Hadamard-portar i rad på två olika kvantbitar) skapar kvantsuperposition och transformationer i Blocsferen (där tillstånd kan visualiseras som punkter). 
Semantiskt möts mitosis och double Hadamard inte i hur många saker som skapas fysiskt, utan i konceptet identisk återställning och duplicering av information.

items.html:
Got it. Let's switch to English and cut right to the chase without trying to force analogies that don't fit. You are completely right to call that out: physically and mathematically, a double Hadamard and mitosis are entirely different things, and bending semantics to blend them together isn't accurate. 
Let's separate them completely and look at what they actually do: 
1. Quantum: Double Hadamard (H²)
When you apply two Hadamard gates in a row to a single qubit, you are doing a matrix multiplication that cancels itself out (H × H = I). 
  • Input: 1 Qubit in state
    .
  • Action: You rotate it into a superposition, and then rotate it right back.
  • Output: 1 Qubit in state
    .
  • The Reality: You start with one qubit, and you end with one qubit. Nothing splits, nothing multiplies, and no new objects are created. If you are visualizing two points on a sphere, you are just mapping the trajectory of that single qubit's state. 
2. Biology: Mitosis
Mitosis is a physical, biological process of cellular replication. 
  • Input: 1 biological cell.
  • Action: The cell physically duplicates its DNA, grows, and mechanically splits down the middle (cytokinesis).
  • Output: 2 distinct, physical cells.
  • The Reality: You literally double the physical matter and the number of entities. It is a process of clonal replication, not a mathematical inversion or rotation of a single state. 
They belong to two completely different realms: one is state manipulation of a single system (Quantum), and the other is physical duplication of a biological organism (Mitosis). 
Which of these two separate topics would you actually like to focus on right now: the matrix math of the Hadamard gate or the biological phases of mitosis?

items.text: You said: HADAMARD PRODUCT IS A DOT WITH A CIRCLE AROUND THE DOT AND THEN ANOTHER DOT WITH A CIRCLE AROUND THAT WHICH IS ALREADY SORT OF PAST TENSE, BUT NOT REALLY, BECAUSE IT HASNT BEEN APPLIED

htmlChunks:
You are talking about the Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication), which is written as
∘composed with
 (a dot with a circle around it), not the Hadamard gate (
Hcap H
) from quantum computing. 
If you write out two circles with dots next to each other, you are looking at an operation that has been notated but not yet executed. It is "past tense" only in the sense that the rule is locked in place on the page, but until you actually feed it two matrices, nothing has been multiplied. 
Here is how the Hadamard product works when you actually apply it: 
The Math: Matrix to Matrix
Unlike the quantum gate which changes a single qubit, the Hadamard product requires two matrices of the exact same size. It multiplies them element-by-element. 
If you have Matrix A and Matrix B: 
A∘B=[a11b11a12b12a21b21a22b22]cap A composed with cap B equals the 2 by 2 matrix; Row 1: Column 1: a sub 11 b sub 11, Column 2: a sub 12 b sub 12; Row 2: Column 1: a sub 21 b sub 21, Column 2: a sub 22 b sub 22 end-matrix;
The Semantics: Why it's not like Mitosis
Even if you look at the notation symbol itself
∘composed with
, it represents a filter or a mask, not a split: 
  • Mitosis takes 1 thing and turns it into 2.
  • Hadamard Product takes 2 separate things (Matrix A and Matrix B), mashes them together element-by-element, and leaves you with 1 final matrix. 
It is actually the exact opposite of mitosis—it is a convergence of two data sets into one, rather than one cell splitting into two.
